Nestlings gain mass rapidly under the sustained provisioning regime typical of this species, with parents making frequent foraging trips to nearby freshwater marshes and coastal shallows. Parents share incubation duties equally, and the biparental care system ensures high hatching success under typical conditions. The newly fledged juvenile exhibits a distinctive plumage pattern that differs from the adult breeding plumage, providing a degree of camouflage against the marsh vegetation during the critical period when flight skills are still developing. Young birds gradually acquire adult-like foraging efficiency through observation and practice, initially relying on parents to locate prey patches. The post-fledging dependence period is a crucial phase during which the juvenile refines its hunting techniques and builds the fat reserves necessary for the energetically demanding first migration. Adult body mass fluctuates seasonally, with individuals being heaviest just prior to egg-laying and lighter during the energetically demanding chick-rearing phase. Foraging ecology during the breeding season centers on small fish species such as killifish, sticklebacks, and young-of-the-year cyprinids, which are captured through plunge-diving in shallow waters. The availability of these prey items directly influences both adult body condition and reproductive success.
